newsitem.title: USA: Reform has U.S. farmers looking at options market.
newsitem.headline: Reform has U.S. farmers looking at options market.

text.p: U.S. farmers are expected to buy more options contracts as a price safety net for this year's crops, the first to be planted since the federal farm act ended decades of subsidies, grain analysts said.
The 1996 act eliminated certain planting restrictions and included plans to phase out price supports that guaranteed farmers a minimum payment per bushel if prices fell.
"The predominant risk management of choice is to buy puts fairly close to "at the market" on new crop corn and beans," said Don Roose, president of U.S. Commodities in Des Moines.
The trend toward options use is good news for the Chicago Board of Trade said Patrick Catania, CBOT senior vice-president of market and product development.

"The options growth has outstripped all the other products here at the exchange," he said. "That's largely due to the erosion of subsidies and the added risk that everyone is facing, not only the farmers."
Last year's record agricultural options volume of 14.5 million contracts was up 68 percent from 1995, CBOT reported. Corn options alone were up 74.5 percent at 6.6 million.
"We're expecting (volume) this year to be just as good if not better than last year," said Chris Manns, a corn options trader with CDM Traders Inc.
"I stand next to (commercial traders) and they are doing a lot of one lot, two lot trades," Manns said. The small amounts suggest the trades are on behalf of farmer customers, he said.
Put options allow farmers to lock in a minimum price and decide later if they want to sell grain at that level. If prices go up, farmers can sell elsewhere for a better price.

Unlike futures contracts that obligate farmers to liquidate their market position or deliver grain before the contract expires, options lock in only the right to sell at a certain price. And much like the government price supports, they can guarantee farmers a minimum payment for their grain.

"The farmer needs to replace that floor of income support with a tool, and the tool that fits that hole is the put," said Bill Biedermann, director of research for Allendale Inc, an Illinois-based agricultural research firm.
Banks have encouraged options use as a means of minimizing risk but only for market-savvy farmers, said David Bunker, senior vice president at Mercantile Bank.
The St. Louis-based bank loans money to farmers in Missouri, Kansas, Iowa and Illinois.

"Farmers have done a good job in the past managing the production risk but now with a lessening reliance on a (price) floor, they need to be looking at ways to manage their marketing risk," Bunker said.

Educational programs attest to the growing interest in options. CBOT, state Farm Bureau offices and private marketing firms offer training programs to farmers. CBOT's Catania said CBOT sessions often draw a full house.
Joe Miller, market analyst with the Indiana Farm Bureau, teaches options seminars across the state.
"Traditionally, farmers have not used puts," Miller said. "Since we have no farm (subsidy) program, they're getting more interested.

"I think the majority of hedging should be done in options," he added. It's a safe way to hedge with very little risk. Even if you're bullish, buy the options. It's not only the safest hedge, it's the most reasonable."
